title: How Many Species?
objective: After this level you can explain how many animal species are known and how many may exist.
summary: About 1.5 million animal species have been described (IUCN, 2025). A 2011 estimate by Mora and colleagues puts all animal species at about 7.8 million, so most are still unnamed.

cards.headline: Scientists have named about 1.5 million animal species. Easy part.
cards.body: Every named species has a description behind it: someone found it, studied it and published it. But how do you count the animals nobody has found yet? One team came up with a clever answer, and it's humbling.

cards.fact: Named so far: about 1.5 million animal species.
cards.context: That's the IUCN Red List's 2025 tally of described animal species, and about 1 million of them are insects. IUCN itself warns that the figures aren't always up to date. So treat it as a snapshot, not a final score.

cards.headline: Counting the ones nobody has seen
cards.body: In 2011, Camilo Mora and colleagues spotted a pattern. Every species sits inside bigger groups, and those bigger groups are much better known. The number of groups at each level followed a steady relationship with the number of species, so the team used it to predict the total: about 8.7 million species of complex-celled life, give or take 1.3 million, and about 7.8 million of them animals.

cards.fact: Most animals have never been named.
cards.context: By Mora's estimate, about 86 percent of species on land and 91 percent in the ocean still await a description. Naming them all the traditional way could take up to 1,200 years and more than 300,000 taxonomists. It's an estimate, not a head count, but the message is hard to miss: you live on a planet you've mostly never met.

mascot.line: Somewhere out there, an animal nobody has named is having a perfectly normal Tuesday.

cards.headline: Species: counted
learned: About 1 million of them are insects
Mora's 2011 estimate: about 7.8 million animal species
Most species on land and at sea are still unnamed

questions.prompt: Roughly how many animal species had been described by 2025, according to the IUCN Red List's tally?

options.label: About 15,000
options.rationale: Far too few for a whole kingdom.

options.label: About 15 million
options.rationale: More than even the estimates of all animals.

questions.explanation: IUCN's 2025 table lists about 1.55 million described animal species.

questions.prompt: How did Mora's team estimate the number of species nobody has found yet?

options.label: They counted every animal in one forest
options.rationale: They used patterns in classification, not a field count.

options.label: They asked museums for their best guesses
options.rationale: The estimate came from a numerical pattern.

options.label: They sampled DNA from seawater
options.rationale: That wasn't the method in this study.

options.label: They used how species counts track bigger groups

questions.explanation: Counts of better-known higher groups follow a steady relationship with species numbers, which let the team predict the total.

questions.prompt: Level 1 put insects in the crowd without backbones. About how many of the described animal species are insects?

options.label: About 7.8 million
options.rationale: That's the estimate for all animals, named or not.

questions.explanation: About 1 million of IUCN's roughly 1.5 million described animal species are insects.
